labels.about: The Great Military Orphanage, founded 1724, rebuilt 1771–78 by Carl von Gontard with its domed tower.
The royal theatre of 1795 on the Canal, by Michael Philipp Boumann. Destroyed in 1945.
A town palace of 1771–72 by Carl von Gontard after the Palazzo Barberini in Rome. Destroyed 1945, rebuilt 2013–16.
The royal stables: built 1685 as an orangery, a stable from 1714, remodelled by Knobelsdorff in 1746 with horse-tamer groups on the roof.
The garrison commander's house on the Lustgarten, 1819 on an older inn. Destroyed 1945.

Built 1730–35 to Philipp Gerlach's design for the garrison; its carillon played from the 88 m tower. Frederick William I and Frederick the Great were buried here. Burnt out on 14 April 1945, demolished 1968.
Karl Friedrich Schinkel's church, built 1830–37; the dome on its colonnaded drum followed 1843–50 under Persius and Stüler. 77 m to the cross.
The town hall, 1753–55, by Jan Bouman after a Palladian model; a gilded Atlas carries the globe on its cupola.
The Catholic parish church, 1867–70, by Wilhelm Salzenberg after a design by Friedrich August Stüler; its campanile follows San Zeno in Verona.
Nave 1726–28 by Pierre de Gayette, tower 1734 by Johann Friedrich Grael, 86 m over the Havel. Burnt 1945; the nave was pulled down in 1961, the tower blown up in 1974.
The Huguenot congregation's church, 1752–53, by Jan Bouman after Knobelsdorff: a small oval temple under a dome.
The Hohenzollerns' town palace, remodelled by Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff 1744–52; the Fortunaportal of 1701 faces the Alter Markt. Burnt out 1945, demolished 1959–60.
A triumphal arch of 1770 by Carl von Gontard and Georg Christian Unger — the town side and the field side were designed differently.
Built 1755 — one of the first neo-Gothic buildings on the European continent.
The hunters' gate of 1733, crowned by a stag brought down by hounds; the oldest of Potsdam's gates still standing.
Knobelsdorff's obelisk of 1753–55, almost 20 m high, its base carrying medallions of the Great Elector and the first three kings.
The pump house that fed the fountains of Sanssouci, built 1841–43 by Ludwig Persius as a mosque, its chimney a 36 m minaret.
The garrison's drill hall of 1734, 167 m long under one roof; Georg Christian Unger's show front of 1781 faces the Breite Straße. Burnt 1945 — the front still stands.
The Great Military Orphanage, founded 1724, rebuilt 1771–78 by Carl von Gontard with its domed tower.
